title: What Happens When Your Nose Runs in the Cold?
sources: Northwestern Medicine HealthBeat, 'Why Does the Cold Weather Make My Nose Run?' (updated December 2025, checked 2026-11-28): 'a study of 90 people visiting a ski-resort clinic found that 96% who were exposed to the cold had some degree of rhinorrhea' (line 2: 'In one ski study, ninety-six percent dripped'); 'When we breathe in, our noses warm the air and add moisture as the air travels down into our lungs' (line 3); 'Cold, dry air irritates your nasal lining, and as a result, your nasal glands produce excess mucus' (line 7): https://www.nm.org/healthbeat/healthy-tips/why-does-the-cold-weather-make-my-nose-run

Harvard Health Publishing, 'You don't say? Why does your nose run in cold weather?' (2021-12-01, checked 2026-11-28): a runny nose in the cold is 'a sign that the nose is doing its job to heat up and moisturize air before it enters the lungs' (line 3: 'a built-in heater for every breath', paying off the previous video's tease): https://www.harvardhealth.org/staying-healthy/you-dont-say-why-does-your-nose-run-in-cold-weather

Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ask Smithsonian: Why Does My Nose Run When It's Cold?' (Alicia Ault, 2016-03-21, quoting allergist-immunologist Mitchell Grayson, Medical College of Wisconsin; checked 2026-11-28): 'Heating the air and mucous production are among the nose's primary activities' (line 3); the drip is 'essentially a nervous system response, mediated by chemical neurotransmitters that control the glands' (line 5: 'a nerve reflex'); 'It's the same system that causes the mouth to water in anticipation of a meal' (line 6); condensation 'joins with the mucous and adds to the outward flow' (director visual only): https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/ask-smithsonian-why-does-my-nose-run-when-its-cold-180958383/

Cleveland Clinic, 'Runny Nose' (checked 2026-11-28): 'Cold, dry air irritates your nasal lining. In defense, your nasal glands produce excess mucus to keep the lining moist, resulting in a runny nose' (lines 5, 7); see a provider if 'Your runny nose or congestion lasts more than three weeks or occurs with a fever' (line 9): https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/symptoms/17660-runny-nose

Baraniuk JN, 'Neural Regulation of Mucosal Function', Pulmonary Pharmacology & Therapeutics 2008 (NIH PMC2796429, checked 2026-11-28): 'exhaled air saturated with water vapor at body temperature passes of the relatively cooler nasal surface', condensing on it; this 'countercurrent recycling mechanism may recover as much at [sic] a third of the water and energy expended in conditioning inhaled ambient air' (line 8, the answer: 'it wins back up to a third'): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2796429/

Baraniuk JN & Merck SJ, 'New Concepts of Neural Regulation in Human Nasal Mucosa', Acta Clinica Croatica 2009 (NIH PMC4209304, checked 2026-11-28): 'Countercurrent condensation of water from exhaled air may recover 30% of the water' used to humidify inhaled air (line 8, second source for the answer): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4209304/

Tease (next video): Cleveland Clinic, '7 Remedies To Heal a Burnt Tongue' (2023-08-01, checked 2026-11-28): 'Taste buds regenerate approximately every two weeks' (line 10: 'taste buds that regrow'): https://health.clevelandclinic.org/how-to-heal-a-burnt-tongue/

lines.text: Ever stepped outside and felt that first drip?
But here's the twist: cold air trips a nerve reflex.
Same one that waters your mouth before a meal.
Answer: it wins back up to a third.
Over three weeks, or a fever? See a doctor.
lines.caps: OVER THREE *WEEKS | OR A *FEVER? | SEE A *DOCTOR
